concept.name: Fama-French three-factor model
concept.definition: An empirical asset-pricing model from Fama and French (1993, 'Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds') that explains stock returns with three factors: the market excess return (Rm-Rf), the size factor SMB, and the value factor HML.
concept.intuition: How a stock moves is largely explained by three dials: how the whole market did, how small caps did relative to big caps, and how cheap (high book-to-market) stocks did relative to expensive ones.
concept.mechanics: R_i - R_f = alpha_i + b_i*(R_m - R_f) + s_i*SMB + h_i*HML + e_i, estimated by time-series regression; factor series are constructed from value-weight portfolios sorted on size and book-to-market using NYSE breakpoints, as distributed in the Kenneth French data library.
concept.formula: R_i - R_f = alpha_i + b_i*(R_m - R_f) + s_i*SMB + h_i*HML + e_i.
concept.failure_modes: The model cannot capture the momentum pattern and leaves other documented anomalies unexplained, which motivated the Carhart and five-factor extensions; its factors are empirical constructs whose risk-versus-behavioral interpretation remains debated.
concept.misconceptions: A near-zero three-factor alpha is not proof a manager added no value in all senses - it only says returns are explained by market, size, and value exposures; conversely, positive alpha may reflect omitted factors rather than skill.
concept.example: Regressing a small-cap value fund's monthly excess returns on MKT, SMB, and HML typically yields large positive s and h loadings, quantifying how much of its performance is just small-value exposure.

citations.source: Kenneth R. French Data Library, Description of Fama/French Factors
citations.section: Construction; reference to Fama and French (1993), Journal of Financial Economics
